speakers.abstract:
For most of my career, my job was writing code.

Today that's a small part of what I do: AI can take care of the implementation. My job now is to formulate the problem for the AI to solve - choose the metrics to optimize and the constraints to respect - then make it fast and easy for the AI to iterate. This sometimes feels like herding the model: cutting off all the bad routes, so its randomness can only push in the direction of the improvement I want. In this talk, I'll review three real-world projects through this lens, and propose practical ways to set up feedback for the model. This is not a software-factory pitch.

I still write code, and my review is often the most important constraint, but I don't think it makes sense to pretend that me writing and reading all the code is the best way to build software anymore. Luckily, in a world where AIs write the code, the human who formulates the problem is more valuable than the human who wrote the code was a year ago.

speakers.talk_title: If coding is solved, what's left?
speakers.abstract:
A lot of code is generated by agents, and with time, manual coding will go away (almost) completely. What are human engineers going to do then? Will we even have human engineers?

Can agents just do all the planning, coding, reviewing, and testing for us? Do humans have something that LLMs don't?

I think there are some hard limits on what can be delegated, and how. While machines can do a lot of very intelligent work, there are things they won't be doing unless Skynet takes over the world.

speakers.talk_title: Agentic Coding in 2026: Watching 300 Engineering Orgs adopting agents
speakers.abstract:
Most of what gets presented about agentic coding is what worked or what we hope will work. This talk is the other column.

2026 was the year several comfortable assumptions failed under load. Engineering organisations would converge on a single tooling. They didn't, and the ones that mandated it found their engineers routing around it. Productivity gains would be self-evident, but controlled measurement found experienced developers running slower while reporting they were faster. Betting on one vendor seemed the safe option, in a year with three separate model-access shutoffs. That cost would stay acceptable, right up until it became a top-three adoption barrier.

A field report on what the industry collectively got wrong, what the evidence actually shows, and which of these are now solved versus merely renamed.

faqs.question: What is Agent Engineering?
faqs.answer: Agent Engineering is the discipline of designing, building, evaluating, and operating AI agents. It focuses on the systems, abstractions, and engineering decisions that shape agent behaviour.

faqs.question: Who should attend this conference?
faqs.answer: This conference is for AI/ML engineers, software engineers, agent framework builders, tooling & infrastructure teams, startup founders, product builders working with LLMs, and researchers translating ideas into systems.

faqs.question: When and where is the conference?
faqs.answer: The first Agent Engineering Conference takes place in London on 16 October 2026 at Everyman, Canary Wharf, London. It is a one-day, single-track conference of ten 30-minute technical talks, with limited seats.

faqs.question: Can I still get a ticket?
faqs.answer: London is fully booked. We are fully booked and it will be busy, but there will be seats for everyone who has a ticket. Everything you need for the day is in the Day guide at https://agentengineering.world/guide

faqs.question: Can I book seats for a team?
faqs.answer: London is fully booked, so we cannot add new seats for a team. If a ticket holder on your team can no longer attend, email events@agentengineering.world before the event about moving their place to a colleague.

faqs.question: Why is there an approval step?
faqs.answer: This is a single track. Everyone sits in the same room for the whole day, so the people beside you are a large part of what a ticket buys. There is a lightweight approval step to keep the room technical and high signal, and it is aimed at people who build, evaluate and operate agent systems. That is what keeps the questions in each session worth hearing and the breaks worth staying for. It is quick: most registrations clear well inside 24 hours. Nothing is charged until you are in, so there is no risk in registering.

faqs.question: How do I get an invoice?
faqs.answer: After payment, open luma.com/settings/payment, choose Download Invoice, and add your company name, billing address, and tax details. Save the PDF for finance. You are only charged once a registration is approved.

faqs.question: What food is provided?
faqs.answer: Tea, pastries and lunch. Dietary needs can be raised on the day.

faqs.question: Is the venue accessible?
faqs.answer: Access follows Everyman Canary Wharf. Please check the cinema's accessibility information at https://www.everymancinema.com/venues-list/x0vpb-everyman-canary-wharf/, or email events@agentengineering.world.

faqs.question: How does Q&A work during talks?
faqs.answer: Five minutes of every session belongs to the audience, built into the schedule rather than borrowed from it. One question per person, per talk. Ask again once everyone else has had a turn. Ninety seconds to ask it. The host will step in and move things on at ninety seconds. No follow-up debates. If an answer opens a longer discussion, continue it with the speaker afterwards. Questions are taken in order. Submit through Slido during the talk, or raise a hand if the queue is empty.

faqs.question: Is there networking after the conference?
faqs.answer: The programme closes at 16:30 and informal networking continues at the venue or at a separate side event.

faqs.question: Can I get a refund or pass my ticket to someone else?
faqs.answer: Tickets are not refundable, and they cannot be transferred without our approval first. If something comes up and you can no longer attend, contact us before the event and we will where possible move your place to a replacement attendee. Because the audience is curated, that person goes through the same lightweight approval, so please do not pass a ticket on until we confirm the transfer. If we cancel the conference, ticket holders are offered a refund. Full detail is in the event terms at https://agentengineering.world/terms

faqs.question: Is there a code of conduct?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it applies to everyone taking part: attendees, speakers, partners, volunteers and organisers. It covers the venue, any social gathering connected to the conference, and our online channels, before and during the event as well as afterwards. Harassment, discrimination and intimidation are not tolerated. If you experience or witness something, you can report it on the day or afterwards to conduct@super-agentic.ai, and reports are handled confidentially with no retaliation against anyone raising a concern in good faith. Read it in full at https://agentengineering.world/code-of-conduct, alongside the event terms at https://agentengineering.world/terms

faqs.question: Who is speaking?
faqs.answer: The lineup: Samuel Colvin, Founder & CEO at Pydantic; Andrey Breslav, Founder at CodeSpeak; Ismail Homan Pelaseyed, Co-founder & CTO at Superagent; Tobie Morgan Hitchcock, Founder & CEO at SurrealDB; Alexander Korchagin, Head of Technology Adoption at JetBrains; Jon Bratseth, CEO at Vespa.ai; Meryem Arik, CEO at Doubleword; Frédéric Barthelet, CTO & Co-founder at Alpic; Stas Bichenko, CEO at Recombine; Jocelyn D'Arcy, CEO at Poindexter Labs. See the published speakers page.

faqs.question: Can I still apply to speak?
faqs.answer: Speaker applications are closed for this edition. The remaining talks are invited by the programme team. Confirmed names appear at https://agentengineering.world/speakers as they are announced.

faqs.question: Is there a call for papers on Sessionize?
faqs.answer: This edition does not have a call for papers on Sessionize or elsewhere. The lineup is invited by the programme team and published at https://agentengineering.world/speakers as each speaker is confirmed.

faqs.question: What topics will be covered?
faqs.answer: The conference focuses on deep technical sessions across Prompt Engineering, Context Engineering, Harness Engineering, Eval Engineering, Memory Engineering, Inference Engineering, Loop Engineering, Protocol Engineering, Graph Engineering, Search Engineering, Agentic Engineering, and Code Engineering, plus program themes like Agent Optimization, Agent Experience (AX), and the Future of Coding.

faqs.question: How is this different from other AI conferences?
faqs.answer: The conference covers the engineering discipline behind AI agents. It is one track of ten technical talks. Sessions are on systems, architectures, and the trade-offs involved, given by practitioners who build and operate agents themselves.

faqs.question: Are there sponsorship opportunities?
faqs.answer: We are not offering a founding, title, or main sponsorship for this edition. The day is a learning conference for practitioners, not a vendor trade show. Companies can still support a focused part of the day such as refreshments, drinks, or recording, with a shoutout at the conference and visibility to the London Agentic AI community (about 5,000 members). Seats are selective and applications are reviewed. Details: https://agentengineering.world/support

faqs.question: Will talks be recorded?
faqs.answer: Yes. Talks are recorded and shared with ticket holders after the day.

faqs.question: Do you cover travel and accommodation costs?
faqs.answer: Unfortunately, no. This conference is a Founders Edition funded by ticket sales and the organiser. We cannot cover travel or accommodation costs for speakers or attendees.

faqs.question: Can I get a visa invitation letter?
faqs.answer: Unfortunately, no. To keep the organisation of this conference manageable, we do not provide visa invitation letters or handle visa-related matters.

hq.summary: Agent Engineering HQ runs the AgentEng conference and technical events in London and San Francisco, and publishes the Agent Engineering manifesto.
hq.cities: Agent Engineering HQ runs San Francisco. London events run with London Agentic AI. Both hold the same standard of technical depth.
manifesto: Agents are not features. They are long-running systems with their own development lifecycle, and they need their own engineering discipline.

Agentic systems behave differently from traditional software. A response can look successful and still fail the task. Behaviour drifts. Trajectories matter as much as outputs. These properties demand a dedicated Agent Development Lifecycle (ADLC), distinct from the traditional software development lifecycle.

The ADLC covers building, testing, deploying, and monitoring agents in production, with iteration and governance running as continuous layers throughout. Production signals feed back into evaluation. Traces drive improvement. Governance keeps the system trustworthy.

Agent Engineering is the practice of designing, building, evaluating, and operating AI agents across that lifecycle. It applies to every category of agent, from coding and research agents to customer-facing, domain-specific, and autonomous multi-agent systems.

AgentEng exists to define and advance this discipline. We bring together the practitioners building the tools, frameworks, and supporting infrastructure that make every phase of the ADLC work in production.

mindset.title: Non-Determinism
mindset.description: Agent systems do not behave deterministically, so reliability has to be engineered around variance in output rather than assumed from the code path.

mindset.title: Intelligent Specification
mindset.description: Agent behaviour follows the specification it is given. Precise task definitions and planning up front produce more predictable results at runtime.

mindset.title: Every Input is an Edge Case
mindset.description: Users can submit any input, so conventional test coverage does not hold. Behaviour is better understood through evaluation against production traffic.

mindset.title: Resource Allocation
mindset.description: Compute, budget and human review are finite resources, and allocating them across agent runs is a core operational concern at scale.

mindset.title: The Reviewer Framework
mindset.description: Engineering work shifts from writing code towards designing the reviewers that check it, using validation loops and automated pull request gates.

mindset.title: Agent Networking
mindset.description: Agents working together need defined communication patterns, with parallel and sequential workflows arranged to avoid conflicting or duplicated work.

truly_yours.title: Why this one is truly yours
truly_yours.text: Most agent conferences answer to sponsors. Their programme is shaped by booths, paid talk slots and vendor pressure, with hundreds of people deciding what gets on stage. We don't have any of that. One organiser curated every talk for one reason only: what engineers building agents actually need to hear. Your ticket paid for the day, so the day belongs to you.

sections.title: Arriving
paragraphs: Doors and registration open at 08:00. Please aim to arrive between 8:30 and 8:45 AM so you have enough time to find the venue, check in, grab some tea or coffee, meet a few people and get seated.
The programme starts at 9:00 AM sharp. Our agenda is very tight, so we cannot delay the start. Please don't plan to arrive at 9:00 itself.
There will be tea, coffee and freshly baked pastries before the programme starts.

sections.title: Getting here
paragraphs: Finding Everyman can be a little tricky if you haven't been there before. If you can get to Canary Wharf Elizabeth line station, you are 80% there.
If you are coming by Jubilee, DLR or car, head to the Elizabeth line station first and follow the video from there. Please watch it before you travel and allow a little extra time for the walk.

links.label: Walk from Canary Wharf Elizabeth line station to Everyman

sections.title: Registration and badges
paragraphs: Registration is on the left-hand side when you arrive at Everyman. You will get your badge and lanyard there. Please wear your badge throughout the day.
Arriving later? Don't worry. James, Gloria (our Associates), Shashi, or a member of the Everyman team will guide you to the right screen.

sections.title: Social area
paragraphs: The bar is the social area throughout the day, for networking.

sections.title: Speaker area
paragraphs: There is a dedicated speaker area close to registration, for speakers to prepare, meet and take a break. Please respect speakers' privacy when they are busy.

sections.title: Lunch and drinks
paragraphs: Lunch is Everyman's special pizzas, with different pizza options and drinks, and plenty to go around. We have kept it simple to keep the organiser's cognitive load (and dietary requirements) under control.
Tea and coffee are available throughout the day.
If you have a serious allergy or a specific dietary requirement, let us know and we will do our best to help.

sections.title: Questions and Q&A
paragraphs: There is dedicated Q&A time in each session. One question per person, per talk, and please keep it focused and concise.
Long questions, personal work problems, or questions mainly there to promote yourself will be discouraged.
Come curious, come prepared, and don't be afraid to ask the difficult question.

sections.title: Photography and content
paragraphs: There will be official photography and some official video recording.
The conference is not a content creation spot for marketing. Please don't film or create content involving other attendees or speakers without their consent.

sections.title: Phones, laptops and work
paragraphs: Please keep your phone on silent during talks.
Laptops are absolutely fine, just be mindful of people around you. If you need to work for a while, feel free to step aside and do it when appropriate.

sections.title: Seating
paragraphs: We are fully booked and it will be busy, but there will be seats for everyone. Please take your seat a few minutes before each session so we can keep the programme on time.

sections.title: Need help on the day
paragraphs: Find James, Gloria, Shashi or the Everyman staff. You can also message Shashi on X or LinkedIn, or tag AgentEngHQ on X or LinkedIn.

sections.title: After-event social
paragraphs: Details will be shared during the day. It will most likely be at the venue, and you buy your own drinks.

09:15 Agentic Coding in 2026: Watching 300 Engineering Orgs adopting agents. Alexander Korchagin. Most of what gets presented about agentic coding is what worked or what we hope will work. This talk is the other column.

2026 was the year several comfortable assumptions failed under load. Engineering organisations would converge on a single tooling. They didn't, and the ones that mandated it found their engineers routing around it. Productivity gains would be self-evident, but controlled measurement found experienced developers running slower while reporting they were faster. Betting on one vendor seemed the safe option, in a year with three separate model-access shutoffs. That cost would stay acceptable, right up until it became a top-three adoption barrier.

A field report on what the industry collectively got wrong, what the evidence actually shows, and which of these are now solved versus merely renamed.

09:50 Inference Engineering for Long-Running Agents. Meryem Arik. As models become more capable and agents become more ambitious, long-running agents require abundant, affordable inference. This talk looks at the engineering behind making that possible, from caching and scheduling to throughput and serving efficiency.

10:25 Software Development as Constrained Optimization. Samuel Colvin. For most of my career, my job was writing code.

Today that's a small part of what I do: AI can take care of the implementation. My job now is to formulate the problem for the AI to solve - choose the metrics to optimize and the constraints to respect - then make it fast and easy for the AI to iterate. This sometimes feels like herding the model: cutting off all the bad routes, so its randomness can only push in the direction of the improvement I want. In this talk, I'll review three real-world projects through this lens, and propose practical ways to set up feedback for the model. This is not a software-factory pitch.

I still write code, and my review is often the most important constraint, but I don't think it makes sense to pretend that me writing and reading all the code is the best way to build software anymore. Luckily, in a world where AIs write the code, the human who formulates the problem is more valuable than the human who wrote the code was a year ago.

What is Agent Engineering?
Agent Engineering is the discipline of designing, building, evaluating, and operating AI agents. It focuses on the systems, abstractions, and engineering decisions that shape agent behaviour.

Agents are not features. They are long-running systems with their own development lifecycle, and they need their own engineering discipline.

Agentic systems behave differently from traditional software. A response can look successful and still fail the task. Behaviour drifts. Trajectories matter as much as outputs. These properties demand a dedicated Agent Development Lifecycle (ADLC), distinct from the traditional software development lifecycle.

The ADLC covers building, testing, deploying, and monitoring agents in production, with iteration and governance running as continuous layers throughout. Production signals feed back into evaluation. Traces drive improvement. Governance keeps the system trustworthy.

Agent Engineering is the practice of designing, building, evaluating, and operating AI agents across that lifecycle. It applies to every category of agent, from coding and research agents to customer-facing, domain-specific, and autonomous multi-agent systems.

AgentEng exists to define and advance this discipline. We bring together the practitioners building the tools, frameworks, and supporting infrastructure that make every phase of the ADLC work in production.

Non-Determinism: Agent systems do not behave deterministically, so reliability has to be engineered around variance in output rather than assumed from the code path.
Intelligent Specification: Agent behaviour follows the specification it is given. Precise task definitions and planning up front produce more predictable results at runtime.
Every Input is an Edge Case: Users can submit any input, so conventional test coverage does not hold. Behaviour is better understood through evaluation against production traffic.
Resource Allocation: Compute, budget and human review are finite resources, and allocating them across agent runs is a core operational concern at scale.
The Reviewer Framework: Engineering work shifts from writing code towards designing the reviewers that check it, using validation loops and automated pull request gates.
Agent Networking: Agents working together need defined communication patterns, with parallel and sequential workflows arranged to avoid conflicting or duplicated work.
